section_summary: This section consists chiefly of public letters urging Secretary of State Cordell Hull and other officials to halt American exports of arms, aircraft, oil, scrap metal, and other war materials to Japan during its invasion of China. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could not bar arms shipments without a presidential finding of a state of war, would then apply equally to China and Japan, and did not authorize embargoes on oil, scrap iron, or ordinary commodities. The section also contains correspondence about Loyalist Spain, newspaper reports of the Japanese attack on a Chinese civilian airliner, missionary testimony about bombing casualties at Hankow and Wuchang, and two church petitions against aiding Japanese aggression.

subfiles.title: Floyd A. Baker to Cordell Hull protesting American supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Baker asks why the United States continues supplying Japan with arms and raw materials while Japan attacks China.
subfiles.summary: Floyd Baker, citing an interview with Sun Fo, argues peace-minded Americans disapprove of policy toward the Sino-Japanese conflict and calls for ending shipments to Japan and aiding China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Floyd A. Baker
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains the legal limits imposed by the Neutrality Act on restricting exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: No proclamation found a state of war between China and Japan, so arms cannot be barred to Japan alone; licenses about $13.8 million to China and $10.6 million to Japan since July 1937; ordinary commodities not covered.

subfiles.title: J. M. Ballowe inquiry on neutrality and the Sino-Japanese conflict
subfiles.about: Ballowe asks whether the President has invoked neutrality and whether American munitions manufacturers face export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: J. M. Ballowe asks whether the President's neutrality power was exercised for China and Japan and what restrictions apply to manufacturers.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to J. M. Ballowe
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost states that the President has not proclaimed a state of war between China and Japan and outlines the remaining licensing rules.
subfiles.summary: The reply says that the Neutrality Act's embargo provisions are inapplicable absent a presidential proclamation, although exporters must obtain licenses. It adds that the government strongly opposes sales of aircraft and aeronautical equipment to forces bombing civilian populations.

subfiles.title: Annette Richards Fallows and others to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The writers urge the United States to stop supporting Japanese aggression against China.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten letter protests Japan's actions in China and questions why the United States cannot halt assistance enabling them. The signatures are partly illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Annette Richards Fallows
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains why neither arms nor scrap iron can be embargoed against Japan under existing law.
subfiles.summary: The reply repeats that an arms embargo would require a presidential state-of-war proclamation and would apply to China as well as Japan. It gives export-license totals and stresses that scrap iron and similar products are outside the Neutrality Act and cannot be prohibited under any existing statute.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Henry W. Peabody to Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Peabody challenges the administration's refusal to recognize a state of war and demands stronger action against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Henry Peabody calls the declared-versus-actual war distinction an evasion, argues a referendum and consistent embargo would check aggression, supports China, and criticizes Congress and the President.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Mrs. Henry W. Peabody
subfiles.about: Yost explains that the Neutrality Act cannot selectively embargo an aggressor nation.
subfiles.summary: Yost says no authority permits stopping arms merely because a nation is an aggressor; the Neutrality Act, if applied, would bar shipments to China and Japan alike.

subfiles.title: Carl E. Mapes forwarding the Hackett protest
subfiles.about: Representative Mapes forwards a constituent letter about exports to Japan and Loyalist Spain.
subfiles.summary: Mapes sends John and Mabel Hackett's letter and promises it will be considered at State.

subfiles.title: Mabel and John Hackett to Carl E. Mapes
subfiles.about: The Hacketts urge a halt to war materials for Japan and permission for arms shipments to Loyalist Spain.
subfiles.summary: The Hacketts ask Mapes to use every means to reverse export policy, calling American participation in violence morally shameful.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull to Carl E. Mapes concerning the Hackett letter
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges the forwarded Hackett letter and supplies a copy of the Department's reply.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Mapes's letter on Spain and the Far East, returns the Hacketts' letter, and encloses his reply.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to John and Mabel Hackett
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the distinct statutory bases for the Spanish arms embargo and policy toward China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reply to the Hacketts: Congress imposed the Spanish embargo in January 1937, ending only by repeal or a finding that strife ceased; no state-of-war proclamation for East Asia, so no lawful Japan-only embargo; license totals.

subfiles.title: Haddonfield correspondent to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The writer condemns American supplies to Japan and attacks the administration's interpretation of neutrality laws.
subfiles.summary: Haddonfield writer cites a Foreign Policy Association survey and Joseph Green to argue a real state of war exists in China and Spain, contrasting military preparations with continued exports.

subfiles.title: “Perfidious Albion!” editorial clipping
subfiles.about: The editorial condemns British appeasement of Hitler and urges the United States to avoid another European war.
subfiles.summary: Editorial clipping 'Perfidious Albion!' portrays Czechoslovakia as the latest state sacrificed by British policy and insists the US should not fight Britain's battles.

subfiles.title: John M. Leyda to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Leyda denounces American war-supply exports to Japan and urges a quarantine.
subfiles.summary: Leyda quotes an AP report that the US supplied 54.4 percent of Japan's 1937 war-material purchases, calls suppliers profiteers, criticizes the neutrality law and Dies Committee, and endorses a quarantine.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to John M. Leyda
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains neutrality law, export statistics, civilian-bombing policy, and the Spanish arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: No legal authority exists for a unilateral arms ban on Japan without a proclamation; condemnation of civilian bombing noted; Leyda referred to earlier letters on the Spain embargo.

subfiles.title: Minnie M. Slawson to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Slawson asks Hull to stop exports of bombs, war materials, and oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Minnie Slawson recounts a Chinese speaker's claim that Japanese bomb wreckage was marked Made in U.S.A.; says an export cutoff could rapidly stop Japanese aggression.

subfiles.title: Fort Worth Star-Telegram reports on the downed Chinese airliner
subfiles.from: Fort Worth Star-Telegram, International News Service, and Associated Press
subfiles.about: The clipping reports recovery of a Chinese airliner attacked by Japanese aircraft and Japan's warning to civilian aviation.
subfiles.summary: Fort Worth Star-Telegram: a Chinese airliner was found in the West River near Macau after Japanese planes allegedly forced it down and machine-gunned passengers; American pilot Hugh Woods survived; Japan claimed mistaken identity.

subfiles.title: Fort Worth Press report on the Japanese attack on a passenger plane
subfiles.from: Fort Worth Press and United Press
subfiles.about: The article reports that Japanese aircraft shot down and strafed a Chinese passenger plane near Guangzhou.
subfiles.summary: Fort Worth Press: twelve of seventeen aboard feared dead, survivors fired upon while swimming; pilot Hugh Woods and passenger C. N. Lo identified; Sun Fo intended passenger.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Minnie M. Slawson
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost addresses neutrality law and the allegation that American-made bombs were being used by Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply repeats that no unilateral Japanese arms embargo is lawful without a presidential state-of-war proclamation. It states that the Department had issued no licenses for exporting bombs to Japan since July 1, 1937, and says the government had directly discouraged American aircraft manufacturers from materially encouraging civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: Presbyterian correspondent to the Secretary of State on scrap exports
subfiles.about: The writer objects to American scrap iron and steel exports that sustain Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: A Presbyterian writer cites 680,000 tons of American scrap going to Japan in early 1938 and over $35 million in 1937, calling continued support inconsistent with Christian statesmanship.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mr. Elliott
subfiles.about: Yost explains why the government cannot embargo scrap iron and steel exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply reviews the absence of a presidential war proclamation and provides licensed-arms export totals for China and Japan. It emphasizes that scrap iron and steel are not statutory implements of war and that no existing law authorizes the President or Secretary of State to prohibit their export.

subfiles.title: Linda B. Mathes to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Mathes requests information about war-material exports to Japan and the arms embargo on Spain.
subfiles.summary: Linda Mathes of the Federated Church Women, Chicago, writes briefly on American exports supporting Japan and the contrasting embargo against Spain.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Linda B. Mathes
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the laws governing the Spanish embargo and arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter says the Spanish embargo was expressly enacted by Congress and could be lifted only by repeal or a presidential finding that civil strife had ended. It contrasts this with East Asia, where no state-of-war proclamation existed, and reiterates both the limits of the Neutrality Act and licensed-export totals.

subfiles.title: May Estelle Cook request for export statistics
subfiles.about: Cook asks for figures on United States exports of munitions and oil.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten request seeks a statement covering recent United States exports. Its principal subjects are munitions and petroleum shipments.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to May Estelle Cook
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost supplies arms-license press statements and redirects Cook's oil inquiry to the Commerce Department.
subfiles.summary: Department sends May Cook monthly press statements on arms and munitions licenses, January to August 1938, noting it keeps no statistics on commodities like oil.

subfiles.title: James M. Yard to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Yard urges Hull to stop American munitions and war supplies from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: James Yard of the Chicago Round Table says reliable information shows Japan could not continue the war many months without American supplies.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to James M. Yard
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost reiterates the legal and policy reasons for not imposing an arms embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter explains that a presidential proclamation would trigger an embargo against both China and Japan, while no legal authority exists for a Japan-only ban. It repeats licensed-export totals and notes that the Neutrality Act cannot restrict commodities outside the statutory arms list.

subfiles.title: W. Russell Bowie to Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Bowie asks whether the State Department will seek action against exports of oil, scrap iron, and other materials essential to Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: Bowie says arms exports to China exceeded those to Japan but ignore Japan's larger strategic purchases, calls policy inconsistent with condemning aggressors, and asks what remedy is planned.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to W. Russell Bowie
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost states that existing law does not authorize an embargo on oil, scrap iron, or similar commodities.
subfiles.summary: Yost refers Bowie to the July 7 letter; future authority to prohibit such exports must come from Congress.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of William M. Danner's letter
subfiles.about: A Senate memorandum refers Danner's views on shipments of war material to Japan to the Secretary of State.
subfiles.summary: Senate referral of William Danner's Los Angeles letter for acknowledgment and consideration.

subfiles.title: William Gibbs McAdoo to William M. Danner
subfiles.about: McAdoo informs Danner that his letter on the Sino-Japanese conflict is being sent to the Secretary of State.
subfiles.summary: McAdoo says administering the Neutrality Act belongs to the executive branch and forwards Danner's protest to State.

subfiles.title: William M. Danner to William Gibbs McAdoo
subfiles.about: Danner asks McAdoo to lead an effort to stop American war materials from sustaining Japan's campaign in China.
subfiles.summary: Danner says Japan's undeclared war rests mainly on American material and presents an export cutoff as a Christian and humanitarian measure.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William M. Danner
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Green explains why the Neutrality Act has not been invoked to stop war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The response says the absence of a presidential state-of-war proclamation leaves no authority to bar arms exports to Japan alone. It explains the President's discretion, gives licensed-arms export totals for both belligerents, and encloses the Joint Resolution.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull to William Gibbs McAdoo
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges McAdoo's referral and encloses the Department's reply to Danner.
subfiles.summary: Hull returns Danner's September 2 letter to McAdoo with a copy of the direct reply.

subfiles.title: Walter R. Agard to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Agard protests American assistance to Japanese aggression and asks for a ban on war-supply exports.
subfiles.summary: Walter Agard urges the administration to turn words into action by prohibiting supplies to Japan, citing humanity and national interest.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Walter R. Agard
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost gives the Department's standard explanation of neutrality law and export policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply says the Neutrality Act could be invoked only through a presidential proclamation and would then embargo China and Japan equally. It supplies comparative license totals and explains that commodities outside the formal arms list cannot be prohibited under the act.

subfiles.title: Missionary letter describing Japanese air raids on Hankow and Wuchang
subfiles.from: Unnamed missionary doctor or hospital worker at Methodist General Hospital, Hankow
subfiles.about: A missionary medical worker recounts civilian casualties, hospital work, and fear during Japanese bombing raids.
subfiles.summary: Missionary letter describes mass casualties from Japanese raids on Hankow and Wuchang, American and British names on bomb fragments, missionaries staying, and depleted hospital staff treating the wounded.

subfiles.title: Petition to the Secretary of State on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.from: Charlotte E. Jones and members of her St. Helena church
subfiles.about: The petition asks the Secretary of State to end American trade that materially supports Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition says Japan has violated the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact and condemns the bombing of undefended cities. It alleges that American planes, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks sustain Japanese aggression and asks for every practical measure to stop the traffic.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Charlotte E. Jones concerning the church petition
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the petition and explains legal limits on embargoing Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that the Neutrality Act would embargo both China and Japan if the President proclaimed a state of war but permits no Japan-only arms ban without that finding. It provides export-license totals, explains that non-arms commodities cannot be prohibited, and reiterates the government's condemnation of civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Charlotte E. Jones's petition
subfiles.about: The White House refers Jones's petition for acknowledgment and consideration.
subfiles.summary: White House routing sheet directing State to acknowledge and consider Charlotte Jones's petition.

subfiles.title: Petition to the President on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.from: Charlotte E. Jones and members of her St. Helena church
subfiles.about: The petition asks the President to end American exports that make the United States a partner in Japan's destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: Closely paralleling the petition to the Secretary of State, it invokes treaty violations, attacks on noncombatants, and American supplies ranging from bombs to scrap iron and oil. The signers appeal to the Good Neighbor principle and ask for direct or indirect action against the trade.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Charlotte E. Jones after White House referral
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the White House referral and points Jones to his earlier response.
subfiles.summary: Yost confirms Jones's September 5 petition and refers her to his September 19 answer on the same matter.

subfiles.title: Lulu R. Kuhns to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Kuhns supports an embargo on metals, machinery, and other munitions sent from the United States to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lulu Kuhns, an Arizona teacher, supports an embargo even at temporary economic loss.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Lulu R. Kuhns
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains why existing law does not permit the proposed export embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply says a presidential state-of-war proclamation would impose an arms embargo on China and Japan alike, while none permits selective restrictions. It repeats comparative arms-license totals and explains that the Neutrality Act cannot prohibit ordinary commodities.

subfiles.title: Charles Bond to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Bond urges the State Department to restrict or prohibit munitions shipments supporting Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Charles Bond says heavy American shipments to Japan lack ethical justification even if legal and should be restricted.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Charles Bond
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost gives the Department's standard legal explanation for continuing exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The response says the President has not proclaimed a state of war, so the Neutrality Act cannot be used to embargo Japan alone and would in any event apply equally to China. It cites licensed-export totals and reiterates that the act covers only enumerated arms, ammunition, and implements of war.
